strengths: The paper introduces a meaningful task: inferring text-specific information-seeking goals from reading behavior, extending prior work on classifying general reading modes.

The strongest selection model provides convincing evidence of predictive signal: RoBERTEye-Fixations achieves 49.3% three-way accuracy versus 33.3% chance, including 49.0% on unseen texts and 47.8% when both texts and participants are unseen.

The evaluation includes article-level text splits, separate participant generalization, ten-fold cross-validation, established gaze–text models, and a trained text-only reconstruction baseline. These are useful experimental design choices.
The manuscript provides extensive implementation details and representation comparisons, and explicitly addresses participant consent, privacy, and limitations affecting deployment.
weaknesses: The evidence for open-ended goal reconstruction is substantially weaker than the framing suggests. On unseen texts, DalEye-Llama obtains question-word/category kappas of only 0.069/0.074, and its QA accuracy of 65.1% is below arbitrary GPT-4o questions at 66.7%. The strongest reconstruction results concern texts whose exact target questions were available during training, so they do not establish reconstruction of previously unseen goals.

The QA reconstruction metric is not a valid equivalence test: answering the original multiple-choice item correctly does not imply that the generated question matches the reader's goal. Incorrect same-span questions already achieve 67.7% on unseen texts. Figure 7 even shows a question about an unsupported 'eponymous village' counted as successful. Direct human assessment of semantic equivalence and a paragraph-plus-answers baseline are needed.

The fine-grained selection evaluations have important interpretation problems. For Different Spans, 55.6% is the uniform three-question random baseline, but always choosing the span associated with two questions achieves 66.7%; labeling 55.3% as 'Chance / Majority' overstates several models' performance. For Same Span, Table 1 excludes predictions of the third question, apparently conditioning evaluation on model output. The paper should clarify this filtering, report coverage, and evaluate forced binary selection on all eligible trials.

Controls do not adequately isolate what gaze information drives performance. The strongest discriminative model lacks matched text-only and within-paragraph shuffled-gaze controls, and there are no targeted ablations separating fixation locations, durations, order, and total reading time. The simple similarity baselines perform near chance and provide limited mechanistic insight.

The training descriptions conflict materially. Section 4.2 and Appendix B describe generative next-token training, and Section 6 says the generative models are not explicitly trained for selection. Appendix C.2 instead describes DalEye-LLaVA training with correct-versus-distractor likelihoods and a classification loss. This changes the interpretation of the discriminative–generative comparison and impedes reproduction.

The methodological contribution is primarily adaptation of existing architectures, with the strongest results coming from an existing gaze–text encoder and the proposed LLaVA variant performing near chance. Combined with evaluation on one laboratory dataset containing only 162 paragraphs and three prescribed goals per paragraph, the unresolved evaluation issues leave insufficient evidence for the claimed breadth and significance at a top-tier venue.

strengths: The task is scientifically interesting: predicting text-specific information needs goes beyond classifying general reading modes. Separating questions with shared versus distinct answer spans provides a useful experimental distinction.

Question selection yields meaningful positive evidence. RoBERTEye-Fixations achieves 49.3% overall accuracy versus 33.3% chance, including 49.0% on unseen texts and 47.8% when both texts and participants are unseen.

The evaluation separates participant and text generalization, holds out texts at the article level, and performs model selection within cross-validation splits. These are appropriate safeguards for this structured dataset.

The paper evaluates several model families, includes a text-only reconstruction baseline and input-representation variants, and documents substantial implementation details. Its ethics discussion addresses consent and potential population biases.
weaknesses: Evidence for open-ended reconstruction of novel goals is substantially weaker than the framing suggests. On unseen texts, DalEye-Llama obtains question-word and question-category kappas of only 0.069 and 0.074. Its QA accuracy of 65.1% is below arbitrary GPT-4o questions (66.7%) and incorrect same-span human questions (67.7%). Gains over the trained text-only baseline exist, but the strongest reconstruction results concern texts whose exact target questions appeared during training.

The reconstruction evaluation does not establish recovery of the reader's actual intent. Section 5.3 treats selecting the original correct answer as necessary and sufficient for valid reconstruction, although unrelated questions can produce that answer through passage and answer-option cues. Figure 7 illustrates this directly: a generated question about an 'eponymous village' receives the correct answer for a question about Lemnos's attractions. Human assessment of semantic equivalence and a passage-plus-options baseline are needed.

The Different Spans baseline is misleadingly labeled 'Chance / Majority.' Uniform three-question guessing gives 55.6%, but always predicting the shared-span group gives 66.7%. Thus, several reported improvements over chance underperform the relevant majority baseline; even the best model's 70.9% represents a much smaller gain. The Same Span evaluation also needs clarification about whether q1 predictions are discarded or candidates are rescored, because conditioning on predictions would create model-dependent evaluation subsets.

Controls do not sufficiently isolate the useful gaze information. The strongest selection model lacks matched text-only, shuffled-gaze, and reduced-feature ablations. Although balanced questions constrain text-only performance, such controls would test implementation shortcuts and distinguish coarse attention localization from finer goal-specific information. The existing generative prompt and representation comparisons do not resolve this.

The training description contains a material contradiction. Section 4.2 and Appendix B.1 describe DalEye-LLaVA as trained autoregressively on the correct question, whereas Appendix C.2 describes a contrastive classification loss over correct and distractor questions. This also conflicts with the explanation that generative models underperform because they are not explicitly trained for selection, making the comparison difficult to interpret or reproduce.

The methodological contribution is mainly adaptation of existing architectures, and the proposed multimodal LLaVA variant performs near chance. Consequently, acceptance depends heavily on a convincing task and empirical contribution. A single controlled dataset with three experimenter-provided questions per paragraph, weak unseen-text reconstruction, and unresolved evaluation issues does not yet provide sufficient support for the broader arbitrary-goal decoding claims.

strengths: The paper introduces an interesting and scientifically meaningful task: inferring text-specific information-seeking goals from reading behavior. Distinguishing questions about the same critical span moves beyond coarse classification of reading modes.

The strongest selection results provide concrete evidence of useful signal. RoBERTEye-Fixations achieves 49.3% three-way accuracy against 33.3% chance, and retains 47.8% accuracy when both texts and participants are unseen. Its 57.3% same-span accuracy suggests some sensitivity beyond identifying relevant passage regions.

The evaluation thoughtfully separates generalization to new participants, new texts, and both. Article-level text splitting, per-split model selection, and mixed-effects comparisons address important dependencies in eye-tracking data.

The study compares several modeling approaches, includes a trained text-only reconstruction baseline, and reports prompt and representation variations. The discussion acknowledges reconstruction limitations, and the ethics section addresses consent, privacy, and population-specific reliability.
weaknesses: Evidence for open-ended reconstruction of novel goals remains weak. On new texts, DalEye-Llama achieves question-word and question-category kappas of only 0.069 and 0.074. Its BERTScore of 0.631 falls below the incorrect same-span question baseline of 0.650, and its QA accuracy of 65.1% falls below arbitrary GPT-4o questions at 66.7%. Gains over the trained text-only model are encouraging, but the strongest reconstruction results concern passages whose questions were available during training.

The QA metric does not establish faithful reconstruction. Selecting the original correct answer after substituting a generated question is neither necessary nor sufficient for semantic equivalence. Incorrect same-span questions already achieve 67.7% on new texts, demonstrating substantial ambiguity in this proxy. Human evaluation of goal equivalence and an answer-only or question-ablated QA control are needed.

The different-span baseline is misleadingly labeled 'Chance / Majority.' Although 55.6% is the correct expectation for uniformly choosing among three questions and then grouping them, always selecting the shared span achieves 66.7%. The best result, 70.9%, therefore improves much less over the relevant majority baseline than the reported comparison suggests. Balanced accuracy would make this evaluation more informative.

The strongest discriminative model lacks matched text-only and shuffled-gaze controls. Balanced questions make the three-way results meaningful, but these controls would strengthen attribution to trial-specific eye movements. Feature ablations would also help establish whether the same-span gain reflects fine-grained temporal behavior or simpler aggregate attention patterns.

The generative training description is internally inconsistent. Section 4.2 describes next-token training on the correct question, whereas Appendix C.2 describes DalEye-LLaVA optimization using the correct question and two distractors. This also conflicts with the explanation that the generative models are not explicitly trained for selection. The actual objective must be clarified for reproducibility and fair interpretation.

The task contribution is stronger than the modeling contribution: adapted existing discriminative models perform best, while the proposed generative approaches are substantially weaker. Combined with evaluation gaps and evidence limited to externally assigned questions in one laboratory corpus, the paper is promising but slightly below the acceptance threshold.

strengths: The paper introduces a meaningful cognitive decoding task: identifying text-specific information-seeking goals from reading behavior. Distinguishing semantic goals extends prior work on classifying general reading procedures.

Goal-selection results provide convincing evidence of useful gaze information. RoBERTEye achieves 49.3% three-way accuracy against 33.3% chance, retaining 47.8% accuracy for unseen texts and participants. Its 57.3% same-span accuracy suggests information beyond coarse localization of relevant text.

The evaluation includes ten-fold cross-validation, article-level text separation, distinct participant/text generalization regimes, established gaze-language models, and matched text-only baselines for the fine-tuned generators. These are substantial experimental strengths.

Feature ablations and cognitive analyses help interpret performance. The appendix provides extensive training details, prompts, and numerical results, while the ethics discussion appropriately addresses consent and potential deployment biases.
weaknesses: The evidence for open-ended reconstruction is substantially weaker than for selection. On unseen texts, DalEye-Llama improves BLEU only from 0.236 to 0.253 and BERTScore from 0.617 to 0.631, without improving question-category accuracy. The strongest familiar-text results involve questions already observed during training or prompting. Thus, the experiments establish constrained goal discrimination more convincingly than recovery of arbitrary goals.

The reconstruction metrics do not establish semantic recovery reliably. In particular, answering the original multiple-choice item correctly is not sufficient to establish that the generated question matches the intended goal: deliberately incorrect same-span questions obtain 67.7% QA accuracy on new texts, versus 68.3% for the best reported generator. Table 16 also contains semantically inappropriate generations scored as successful. Blinded human judgments of goal equivalence and question-ablated QA controls are needed.

Gemini few-shot lacks a matched text-only few-shot baseline. For new participants, its ten demonstrations come from the test paragraph and expose its candidate questions. Comparing this condition with an arbitrary-question baseline confounds gaze information with access to demonstrations and candidate formulations. Identical demonstrations with gaze removed or exchanged would provide a much stronger control.

The Different Spans baseline is mislabeled. Although uniformly choosing among three questions yields 5/9 span accuracy, always choosing the span associated with two questions achieves 2/3. Consequently, 70.9% represents roughly a 4.2-point gain over the span-majority baseline, and Haller RNN's 65.6% does not exceed it. The claim that majority and chance coincide does not hold for this grouped evaluation.

The feature ablations retain fixation-to-word alignment, including in the 'Only Linguistic Text Features' condition. They therefore do not directly establish the claimed importance of temporal ordering. Shuffled-order, fixation-count-preserving, and within-paragraph exchanged-scanpath controls would distinguish sequence information from repeated attention to particular words.

The contribution is primarily a task formulation and empirical study using adapted models, with evidence restricted to one dataset containing three externally assigned questions per paragraph. Broader claims about arbitrary intentions and real-time applications remain untested. Reproducibility is also incomplete in the supplied manuscript because the dataset and code URLs in the reproducibility statement are blank.

strengths: The paper introduces a meaningful task: decoding text-specific information-seeking goals from gaze, extending prior work on classifying general reading modes.

Goal-selection results provide concrete evidence of useful gaze information. RoBERTEye achieves 49.3% three-way accuracy versus 33.3% chance, including 47.8% when both participants and texts are unseen. Its 57.3% same-span accuracy suggests some discrimination beyond identifying the relevant passage region.

The evaluation includes ten-fold cross-validation, article-level text separation, participant generalization, multiple model families, text-only generation baselines, feature ablations, and prompt variations. These are substantial experimental strengths.

The cognitive analysis connects model performance to interpretable reading behavior. The ethical discussion appropriately addresses consent, identification risks, and limitations for populations outside the dataset.
weaknesses: The reconstruction evaluation does not convincingly establish recovery of the intended goal. Question-word and category matches are coarse, and successful downstream QA is neither necessary nor sufficient for semantic equivalence. Incorrect same-span questions already obtain 67.7% QA accuracy on new texts, versus 68.3% for few-shot Gemini. Table 16 even counts the unrelated question 'What is one thing to note about the eponymous village?' as successful. Direct human assessment of goal equivalence is needed.

The strongest generation results concern previously seen paragraphs and questions. For new participants, Gemini receives ten demonstrations from the test paragraph, exposing its possible questions; the fine-tuned models also encounter those questions during training. This is a legitimate evaluation setting, but primarily supports selection or retrieval of known goals. On unseen texts, gains are considerably smaller: DalEye-Llama's BLEU increases from 0.236 to 0.253 over its text-only counterpart, while question-category accuracy does not improve.

Gemini lacks a matched few-shot text-only control using the same demonstrations. Comparing its few-shot gaze condition with an arbitrary text-only question confounds gaze information with demonstration access, particularly when demonstrations contain the target paragraph's questions. Shuffling gaze across goals within a paragraph would further test whether performance depends on the correct gaze–goal association.

The Different Spans baseline is mislabeled as both chance and majority. Uniform random choice among three questions yields 55.6%, but the merged span classes have proportions one-third and two-thirds, so majority-span prediction achieves 66.7%. RoBERTEye's 70.9% remains encouraging, but its improvement over this baseline is much smaller than the presentation suggests. Balanced accuracy and per-span recall would clarify the result.

The scope is narrower than the framing of arbitrary, open-ended goals suggests: one English dataset, 162 paragraphs, and three externally assigned questions per paragraph. The modeling contribution largely adapts existing architectures. Together with the unresolved generation controls and evaluation validity, this leaves the broader contribution slightly below the acceptance threshold despite the credible selection results.

Reproducibility details are extensive, but the submitted reproducibility statement leaves the dataset and code URLs blank. The cited dataset remains identifiable, whereas access to the claimed implementation cannot be verified from the manuscript.

strengths: The paper introduces a meaningful cognitive decoding task: identifying text-specific information-seeking goals from gaze, extending prior work on classifying predefined reading procedures. The distinction between goal selection and free-form reconstruction is useful.

Goal-selection results provide convincing evidence of informative gaze signals. RoBERTEye achieves 49.3% three-way accuracy versus 33.3% chance, including 49.0% on unseen texts and 47.8% on unseen texts and participants. Distinguishing questions sharing a critical span is particularly interesting, although harder.

The evaluation thoughtfully handles participant and text generalization, uses article-level splits and per-split model selection, and accounts for participant and paragraph variability through mixed-effects analyses. Comparisons include established gaze models, several LLMs, text-only generation controls, and feature ablations.

The cognitive analysis connects decoding performance to interpretable reading behavior. Detailed implementation information and an explicit discussion of consent, privacy, and population biases are additional strengths. Overall, the task contribution and selection results support marginal acceptance.
weaknesses: Evidence for precise open-ended reconstruction remains limited. On unseen texts, DalEye-Llama improves BLEU only from 0.236 to 0.253 and BERTScore from 0.617 to 0.631 over its text-only counterpart, without improving question-category accuracy. Human questions explicitly targeting the wrong goal but sharing its critical span outperform every model on these two metrics. The claims should distinguish recovering topical relevance from recovering the reader's specific question.

The reconstruction metrics do not establish semantic equivalence. Question words and categories are coarse, and the stated 'if and only if' interpretation of downstream QA success is unjustified: a different question can still elicit the correct answer option. Indeed, incorrect same-span questions obtain 67.7% QA accuracy on unseen texts. A blinded human evaluation of intent equivalence, alongside question-free QA controls, would substantially strengthen this contribution.

Gemini's strongest reconstruction results require qualification. In the New Participant regime, its demonstrations contain questions and gaze trajectories for the same paragraph, making the setting closer to recovering demonstrated alternatives than unrestricted generation. This is permitted by the protocol, but comparison against an arbitrary zero-shot question does not isolate gaze's contribution. A matched few-shot text-only baseline is missing.

The Different Spans baseline is mislabeled. Uniform random selection among three questions yields approximately 55.6% after grouping, but always choosing the span associated with two questions yields 66.7% on balanced question data. Thus, 70.9% is approximately 4.2 percentage points above the grouped majority baseline, rather than 15.6 points. This does not invalidate the three-way result, but materially changes interpretation of the span-level result.

The demonstrated scope is narrower than arbitrary real-world reading goals: one controlled English dataset, short passages, externally assigned comprehension questions, and laboratory eye tracking. The modeling innovations are mainly adaptations of existing architectures. Additionally, the supplied manuscript leaves the code URL blank, limiting verification despite otherwise detailed implementation documentation.
